name: Bladder cancer
definition: Bladder cancer is a cancer that starts in the bladder, the organ that stores urine.
overview: Blood in the urine is the most common sign of bladder cancer, and it is usually painless. Most people who notice blood in their urine do not have bladder cancer, but the NHS says it still needs checking by a GP. Smoking is the biggest known risk factor. Treatment depends on the type, size and position of the cancer and whether it has spread, and may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy or immunotherapy.
causes: Smoking is the biggest risk factor, and the NHS estimates it causes more than a third of all cases
Contact with certain chemicals at work is also linked to the cancer
Long-term or repeated urinary tract infections and long-term bladder stones are other linked factors
riskFactors: Exposure to certain chemicals in the workplace
Having a close relative with bladder cancer, or having diabetes
signs: Visible blood in the urine, which can look pink, red or sometimes brown
Blood that is only found on a urine test (microscopic blood)
Frequent urination or pain when passing urine
complications: The cancer can come back after treatment, particularly early-stage disease that grows only in the bladder lining
Early-stage cancer can progress to cancer that grows into the bladder muscle
Bladder-lining immunotherapy (BCG) can cause urgency, frequent urination, pain on passing urine and pelvic pain
diagnosis: A GP typically tests a urine sample for blood and infection, and may arrange blood tests including kidney function and blood counts. If bladder cancer is suspected, a referral to a urologist, a specialist in the urinary tract, is usual. The main hospital test is a cystoscopy, in which a thin camera is passed through the urethra to look inside the bladder. Imaging such as a CT urogram may also be used, and abnormal areas can be removed in an operation called TURBT so they can be examined for cancer.
treatment: Treatment depends on the type, size and position of the cancer and whether it has spread. Surgery is usually the first treatment offered, and chemotherapy, radiotherapy, immunotherapy and targeted medicines may also be used. For early-stage disease, treatments placed directly into the bladder, such as BCG or mitomycin, are options. More advanced cancer may involve surgical removal of the bladder, called cystectomy, or radiotherapy with chemotherapy.
prevention: Smoking is the biggest known risk factor, and the NHS links chewing tobacco too. Workplace chemicals are also linked to the cancer.
seekCare: The NHS advises seeing a GP as soon as possible for blood in the urine, even if it comes and goes. Most people with blood in their urine do not have bladder cancer, as infections, kidney or bladder stones and an enlarged prostate are common causes, but it still needs checking.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of bladder cancer?
sections.body:
Blood in the urine is the most common sign of bladder cancer, and it is usually painless. The NHS says visible blood can look pink, red or sometimes brown. Blood may also be present in amounts too small to see, and then it is found only on a urine test.

Other possible signs include passing urine often, pain when passing urine, low back or pelvic pain, and urinary infections that keep coming back. Many of these symptoms have causes other than cancer.

The NHS says blood in the urine still needs to be checked even if it comes and goes. Common causes of blood in the urine include a urinary tract infection, a kidney infection, kidney stones and an enlarged prostate gland. Most people with blood in their urine do not have bladder cancer.

sections.heading: What causes bladder cancer, and who is at higher risk?
sections.body:
Smoking is the biggest risk factor for bladder cancer. The NHS estimates that more than a third of all cases are caused by smoking, and it also links chewing tobacco to the cancer. Exposure to certain chemicals in the workplace is another recognised link. Tobacco smoke and workplace chemicals are the two exposures that the NHS summary highlights most.

The NHS lists several other factors that can raise the risk. They include being a man, having a long-term urinary catheter, having had radiotherapy for cancer, being overweight, having a close relative with the disease and having diabetes. Long-term or repeated urinary tract infections and long-term bladder stones are also linked.

Having a risk factor does not mean a person will develop bladder cancer.

sections.heading: How is bladder cancer diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP typically tests a urine sample for blood and infection. Blood tests, including checks of kidney function and blood counts, may also be arranged. If bladder cancer is suspected, a referral to a urologist, a specialist in the urinary tract, is usual.

At hospital, the main test is a cystoscopy, in which a thin camera is passed through the urethra to look inside the bladder. A biopsy, which is a small sample of tissue, is usually taken during the same procedure. Imaging such as a CT urogram may also be used.

If abnormal areas are found, an operation called TURBT can remove them so that they can be tested for cancer. The National Cancer Institute also describes diagnosis as a combination of tests that look for and examine abnormal areas in the bladder.

sections.heading: How is bladder cancer treated?
sections.body:
Treatment depends on the type, size and position of the cancer and whether it has spread. Surgery is usually the first treatment offered. Chemotherapy, radiotherapy, immunotherapy and targeted medicines may also be used. Doctors describe early-stage and more advanced disease differently, and the usual treatments differ between them.

For cancer that is still confined to the bladder lining, surgery with TURBT removes the tumour, which is often followed by chemotherapy given directly into the bladder. Immunotherapy with BCG, or treatments such as mitomycin, can also be placed directly into the bladder in early-stage disease.

More advanced cancer may involve surgical removal of the bladder, called cystectomy, or radiotherapy combined with chemotherapy. A published review describes radical cystectomy as removing the entire bladder.

sections.heading: Can bladder cancer come back, and what is living with it like?
sections.body:
A published review says early-stage disease that grows only in the bladder lining carries a high risk of recurrence after TURBT. The same review says some early-stage cancers can progress to cancer that grows into the bladder muscle. For this reason, follow-up after treatment is part of care.

Treatment into the bladder can have side effects. A review of BCG treatment says it commonly causes urinary urgency, frequent urination, pain on passing urine and pelvic pain. Another review notes that these symptoms can affect quality of life and sometimes lead to treatment being stopped.

The same literature notes that removing the whole bladder is major surgery that can have long-lasting effects on quality of life.

faqs.q: Is blood in the urine always bladder cancer?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says most people with blood in their urine do not have bladder cancer. Common causes include urinary tract infections, kidney infections, kidney stones and an enlarged prostate gland. It still needs to be checked by a GP, even if it comes and goes.

A cystoscopy is the main hospital test for bladder cancer. A thin camera is passed through the urethra to look inside the bladder. If abnormal areas are seen, a biopsy is usually taken so the tissue can be tested for cancer.

Smoking is the biggest risk factor for bladder cancer. The NHS estimates that more than a third of all cases are caused by smoking. Chewing tobacco is also linked, as are some chemicals used in workplaces.

faqs.q: What treatments are used for bladder cancer?
faqs.a: Treatment depends on the type, size and position of the cancer and whether it has spread. Surgery is usually the first treatment offered. Chemotherapy, radiotherapy, immunotherapy and targeted medicines may also be used.

A published review says early-stage disease that grows only in the bladder lining has a high risk of coming back after TURBT. Some of these cancers can progress to cancer that grows into the bladder muscle. Doctors plan treatment and follow-up with this in mind.
